argument: Hume argues that legitimate knowledge falls into only two categories -- abstract/formal reasoning and empirical matters of fact -- and applies this radical empiricism to dismantle unearned assumptions about the soul and the self. Rather than denying a soul outright, he grants it provisionally and then asks why it must be immortal or personally 'ours,' and when he looks inward for a unified self he finds only a shifting 'bundle' of perceptions with no observed owner, undercutting Descartes's cogito. Since causation itself can't be proven with certainty, Hume concludes that all belief is ultimately a matter of custom and evidence rather than certainty, making him the logical endpoint of the rationalist-to-empiricist lineage running from Descartes through Locke and Berkeley.
keyIdeas: Hume's Fork divides legitimate knowledge into 'relations of ideas' (abstract/formal reasoning like logic and math) and 'matters of fact' (empirical claims); anything else is 'sophistry and illusion.'

Hume's characteristic method is targeted skepticism: rather than flatly denying a concept like the soul exists, he provisionally grants it and then attacks the unearned attributes people attach to it afterward.

Hume argues by analogy that even an immortal soul shouldn't be assumed to concern us: the matter making up our bodies existed before birth and continues after death without 'concerning' us now, so why assume a soul would?

Introspecting, Hume finds no unified, persisting self -- only a 'bundle' of shifting thoughts and perceptions with no observed possessor, which challenges Descartes's inference from 'there is thinking' to 'there is a thinker.'

Since we can't logically prove causation, Hume proposes custom -- repeated, predictable association through observed experience -- as our best available basis for expecting regularities to continue, summed up in 'a wise man proportions his belief to the evidence.'
